theme: God is our refuge, Hezekiah’s psalm
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 46. You have read it before, but read it now as the song Jerusalem sang after the night the Assyrian army fell. Notice the river, the refrain, and the command in verse 10.
settingTheScene: Psalm 46 is a song of the sons of Korah. Many readers connect it to the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib, which you have just read. A city with no great river, Jerusalem is given a river in this psalm, a stream whose waters make glad the city of God. Martin Luther’s hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God” was inspired by it.
observation: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (v. 1).
“Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea” (v. 2).
“There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High” (v. 4).
“God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns” (v. 5).
“The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts” (v. 6).
“The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (v. 7).
“He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear” (v. 9).
“Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm has three stanzas, each ending with a refrain, though the refrain is missing from the first stanza in our texts. The first describes the cosmos in chaos: earth giving way, mountains slipping into the sea, waters roaring. These are pictures of the greatest disaster the ancient mind could imagine. And the response is: “We will not fear.” The reason is not that the danger is small, but that God is a refuge, a very present help.

The second stanza turns to the city. In contrast to the roaring sea is a quiet river. The sea in ancient thought was a symbol of chaos, but Jerusalem has a stream that makes glad the city of God. This is a picture of God’s presence that gives life. And “God will help her when morning dawns.” Recall the 185,000 who lay dead in the morning. The help came at daybreak. The nations rage, but a single word from him melts the earth. The refrain says: “The LORD of hosts is with us.” It is the name Immanuel in the language of the psalms.

The third stanza invites us to look: “Come, behold the works of the LORD.” He makes wars cease, breaks the bow, shatters the spear, burns the chariots. What does that look like? It looks like an empty Assyrian camp.

Then the voice of God himself: “Be still, and know that I am God.” This is not a gentle suggestion to relax, though it may include that. The Hebrew word means “cease striving.” It is addressed to the nations as well as to Israel. Stop fighting, and know who is God. In Hezekiah’s case, the king was told to be quiet and the army to be silent. God did the fighting. The call to stillness is a call to trust, to stop relying on our own efforts and to rest in the one who is exalted among the nations.
connection: Jesus calmed the sea with a word (Mark 4:39), showing that he is the one who rules the chaotic waters. Romans 8:31 asks, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Revelation 22:1 describes a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the true fulfillment of the river of the city of God. Hebrews 12:28 says we receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Matthew 28:20 echoes: “I am with you always.”
application:
Say the refrain, “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress,” every time you feel afraid today.

Practice verse 10. Sit in stillness for five minutes and simply know that he is God.

Think of a “morning” when God helped you after a long night. Thank him.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what in your life feels like the earth giving way.
Thank him that he is a very present help.
Be still before him for a moment.
